text: I outlined the architecture.  But I have some doubts about the form of the logic rules.  You have proposed a set of optimal logic rules for TTT.  They make perfect sense, but are they the most "natural" to emerge out of deep learning?   I find the question not easy to answer.  Or shall we just proceed to run some experiments?

I also suggested an idea to represent the board with (x,y) coordinates where each coordinate ranges in {1,2,3} and the numbers 1,2,3 are purely "symbols" without arithmetic properties (arithmetics is expected to emerge later in AGI).  Perhaps we can "mould" the proposed rules to look more like these "natural form" that are easier to emerge, and that in turn guides us to design the algorithm better?

We wasted a lot of time on the Transformer baseline, it still has some silly bugs.  I want to postpone that and do the logic experiment now...  the architecture of the auto-encoder can be multiple layers with simpler rules near the input and output layers and complex rules in the middle.  Perhaps we don't aim at solve TTT optimally, but just try to confirm that some good rules do emerge in our experiment?

You're right, the current design looks good.  Shall we do the experiments again with this new design, like 4-5 questions ago, before I asked about the string diagrams?

last time you suggested to "move to RL", I wonder how this might work, in particular, I want to retain the ability to train by autoregression even after training by RL.  How might the two algorithms co-exist?

I am hoping that autoregression (AR) enables to form some concepts about the game which can describe the game dynamics (and thus predict its moves and winning or losing).   Then RL would utilize those concepts to make its decisions.  The RL part indeed requires new logic rules to be learned.  I wonder what would be a principled way to combine RL and AR?  In order to earn more rewards, an agent would need to value (increase the Q values of) propositions that correctly describe the world -- this part coincides with AR.
One more question, does the word "variational" mean as in "variational methods"?
Great!!  Please proceed step by step to implement your proposal.
Thanks, I consider that a major breakthrough.  What do you think of the prospect of expanding this model (AR + RL, logic networks) to train on LLM data sets and as an attempt to build AGI?

Thanks, you may create a .md to record our ideas.  You rasied 2 technical questions:
1) Matching of WM to rules.  We can map rules to the state space by a function ⍴.  Rules that are most likely to match a state x would be mapped close to x.  So we can easily collect / make a sample of such rules.  The function ⍴ would be learnable.  By the way, this problem seems essentially same as the recommendation systems problem.
2) State space explosion.  A proposition made of 3-4 symbols with each symbol of dimension "D_model" seems too big to be output at once, on a computer.  Current LLMs solved this problem by outputting 1 token at a time.  The conditional probability of P(token | context) is equivalent to the probability distribution over all sentences / propositions.  This seems to be the tricky part.  Or do you have a better solution?

Great.  Can you explain a bit more about options C and D?  If the embedding dimension of symbols is large, can our current logic network still work unchanged?  Why / where is VQ needed?  How do you get the estimate of 8K?

Yes please update the .md, although I have not fully grasped.  It seems incredible that 8~10K propositions are sufficient to represent the complex world.  But we can have many propositions jointly describing a single situation.  Do we restrict to triples or quadriples of words?  How about a situation like "the black cat is chasing the white cat, the white cat jumped on the green mat but the black cat jumped on the blue mat"?  How to distinguish which cat is which?

Excellent.  But then it would need an ability to create new logic constants such as "cat_1", which I don't think our current network can do that?  Would the constants exist in the same embedding space as other symbols / tokens?

The last similarity example seems to violate some kind of triangular inequality, doesn't it?  It's a great idea that variables bind to entities instead of embeddings.  So entities can be represented by integer indices...

Thanks a lot.  Your help is amazing.  I guess we should start a new repo under the same parent directoy, call it "AGI-experiments".  Transfer some of the files here to there if they could be useful for future reference.  We would be training on text corpora instead of TTT.
In the SCALING_TO_AGI.md, towards the end, it's a bit confusing and I did not follow through.  You seem to have raised a very interesting point:  the idea that "variables" can serve the role of "entities," which is new to me.  In classical logic-based AI, X? and cat_1 are treated differently.  X?'s scope spans within a single logic rule, but cat_1's scope may last for the entire scenario and even for some time period.  This seems complicated and we could explore next.  First let's create the new repo.
